titleStmt.title: Be American and The Lonesome Mermaid
titleStmt.author: Carlos Bulosan
titleStmt.editor: Naomi Roper, Ioana Cheldiu, Alice Leppert, Alice Wagar, Blythe Windle, Poe Claudio

publicationStmt.p: These are transcriptions and encoded versions of 'Be American' and 'The Lonesome Mermaid' by Carlos Bulosan.Our goal with this project is to make his typed drafts of these short stories available digitally as well as more readable.

sourceDesc.p: Transcribed from papers kept by Bulsan that are now held in UW Special Collections. The files used were originally typed on a typewriter and feature handmade corrections by the author.

'Be American' and 'The Lonesome Mermaid' are short stories by Filipino-American author and poet, Carlos Bulosan. 'Be American' tells the story of a narrator trying to help his cousin (a Filipino immigrant) adjust to live in the US.'The Lonesome Mermaid' is a fantasy following a child (presumably in the Philippines) who observes a strange man in his village who claims to be in love with a mermaid who has been kidnapping promising young men.

p.said: Well, I could have told you. But I wanted you to learn.
At least I speak better English now.
This is a country of great opportunity.

body.p: Silence.

You have a wonderful dream, cousin, he told me and left. He left
Los Angeles for a long time. Then, two years later, I received a crate
of oranges from him. The freight mark was San Jose. Now I knew he was
working and had learned the unwritten law of the wanderers on this
troubled earth. So as I ate the oranges, I recalled his last state-
ment: You have a wonderful dream, cousin…

I had a wonderful dream. But I dreamed it for both of us, for
many of us who wandered in silence. Then the boxes and crates became more frequent. Then a barrel of
salmon came from Alaska. And, finally, the letters came. My cousin
Consorcio, the one-time illiterate peasant from the vast plains of
Luzon, had indeed become an American without knowing it. He His letters
were full of wondering and pondering about many things in America.
Now he realized his naivete when he had landed in San Francisco. But
he realized also that he could not ask too much in a strange land.
And it was this realization that liberated him from his peasant pri-
"Be American" 8son, his heritage, and eventually led him to a kind of work to which
he dedicated his time and life until the end.

I was in Oregon when I received a newspaper from Consorcio, post-
marked Pismo Beach. It was the first issue of his publication for
agricultural workers in California. It was in English. From then on,
I received all issues of his publication. All of the five years that
it existed depending defending the workers and upholding the rights and liberties
of all Americans, native or foreign born, so that, as he began to un-
derstand the nature of American society, he became more belligerent in
his editorials and had to go to jail a few times for his ideas about
freedom and peace.

Yes, indeed Corsorcio: you have become an American, a real Ameri-
can. And this land that we have known too well is not yet denuded by
the rapacity of men. Rolling like a beautiful woman with an overflow-
ing abundance of fecundity and murmurous with her eternal mystery,
there she lies before us like a great mother. To her we always return
from our prodigal wanderings and searchings for an anchorage in the
sea of life; from her we always draw our sustenance and noble thoughts,
to add to her glorious history.

But the war came. And the war ended Consorcio’s newspaper work
and his crusade for a better America. And it ended his life also.
When he was brought back from overseas, he knew he would not last long.
But he talked the way he had written his editorials, measured sentences
that range like music, great poetry, and soft, soft. He would not shed
a tear; but his heart must have been crying, seeing eternal darkness
coming toward him, deep, deep in the night of perpetual sleep. Yes,
he would not shed a tear; but he must have been crying, seeing that
there was so much to do with so little time left. There was in his
"Be American" 9voice a kindness for me - unhappy, perhaps, that he could not impart
what he had learned from his wanderings on this earth: unhappy, also,
because he knew that it would take all the people to unmake the un-
happiness which had caught up with us. And now, fifteen years after
his arrival in San Francisco, he was dying.

And he died. But at least he received his most cherished dream:
American citizenship. He did realize later that he had become an
American before he received his papers, when he began to think and
write lovingly about our America. He gave up many things, and finally
his own life, to realize his dream.

But Consorcio is not truly dead. He lives in my undying
love for the American earth. And soon, when I see the last winter
coming to the last leaf, I will be warm with the thought that another
wanderer shall inherit the wonderful dream which my cousin and I had
dreamed and realized in America.

body.p:
There was a deep silence for a minute. The men looked at each other for
a sign of action. Then the mayor ran across the yard and jumped on his horse.
And the other men followed him, riding at full speed through the silence of the
night.

Then I ran to my uncle’s house and woke him up. Then together we ran to
the river, where the sound of agitated men pierced the dark night.

“I have never seen a mermaid, nephew,” shouted my uncle. “I’m glad you
woke me up. This is the night of all nights. I want you to remember it as
long as you live, because you might never see another mermaid again.”

“Maybe there are some mermaid running loose in the world,” I said. “I
understand you could see them walking in broad daylight in the big cities.”

“Those are mermaids of the land, nephew,” he said. “There are many of
them. But the one we are going to see is a mermaid of the water, and it is
not very often that we see them.”

“Maybe so,” I said. “I would like to see a mermaid, of the land or of
the water.”
“I would, too,” he said. “So let’s run like hell, nephew!”

We ran like hell. We found the mayor and the other men crouching behind
the tall reeds in the dry bottom of the river. The stranger was sitting at
the edge of the water on the opposite side of the river. The small lantern
was flickering beside him.

But we could see him. The moon was full and bright. And the air was
very still. Suddenly, he blew out the lantern and thick clouds appeared
from somewhere and covered the moon. And the darkness that had descended
upon the world was so thick we had to join hands in order not to get lost.
And the river suddenly rose up violently, then ebbed away with a deadening
roar. When the moon came out the stranger was gone. THere was only the
soft noise of the receding river and the vanishing phosphorescence of the
bright water. And an unidentified man conjectured about the stranger’s
disappearance.
“Maybe he jumped in the river and couldn’t swim,” said the mayor.
“Maybe he ran to the bushes on the other side of the river,” Father said.
“Maybe he killed himself,” said my uncle.
“Lets look for his body,” suggested the mayor.
“There is no hurry,” said the runner. “He is probably dead now.”
“We will look for his body tomorrow,” said the mayor. “Poor man.”
No man was satisfied. But the crowd dispersed.

But in the morning, the body could not be found. The mayor sent several
divers to the bottom of the river, and they came up with a few bright peb-
bles and edible weeds and water plants. Then there were heated arguments
about the stranger’s disappearance. Some claimed that he had played a trick
on us, but the others thought that he was hiding somewhere in the rice fields
across the river. But we went home and forgot all about him.

Then many years passed. A war broke out somewhere and took most of the
young men away. And after the (unintelligible) famine devastated our town. Then a
terrible plague came and destroyed almost everything alive. But a new ge-
neration grew up and laughed when they were told about the stranger and
the mysterious mermaid.

I was already a man when the stranger appeared again. I was walking on
our street when I met him by accident. And I could not believe my own eyes.
He was still a man of the same uncertain age, as though I were now the older
person.

“Are you the stranger who was supposed to have disappeared with the mer-
maid years ago?” I asked.

“Yes, son,” he said. “But I don’t remember seeing you around when I was
here.”

“It was a long time ago,” I said. “I was only a little boy when you went
away.”

“Have I been gone that long, son?” he asked. “We have no time under the
river."
“Did you really go away with the mermaid?” I asked.
“Yes,” he confessed. “I love her, and she loves me.”

“You are a lucky man,” I said. “I wish I were you. “I’m tired of living
in grass houses and working all day in the hot sun. And look how I am get-
ting old, while you are still the same age as when you left, if not younger.”

“That is human life,” he said. “We are born to do something, but the
arrangement of things in the world compels us to do what we are not fit for.
Some men are fortunate, others are not. Some become great leaders of men,
others become great lovers. But there are many degrees of greatness in seeking beauty,
and another greatness in knowing the truth. But the greatest greatness of all,
my son, is in seeking, sharing, giving love to one who seeks it and gives
it to another man as a token of living greatly and dying the same. I don’t
really know where you fit in the confused scheme of things, but I guess you
will find it in your time.”
“I am terribly afraid of the future,” I said.

“Life is a great adventure,” he said wisely. “Choose your own weapons
and your own hunting ground. I guess your luck will come somewhere on the
way.”
“I’ll keep on hoping,” I said. “And thank you for giving me courage.”

“Don’t despair, son,” he said. “It is not our doing that we are born
on this troubled earth. But it is not also our undoing that we must suffer
under these stars. Look now: it is not our individual lives that count in
the world. It is what goodness and beauty we contribute to life itself.
For my part, I have sacrificed my own life among men for a timeless one.
Yet I know that it is far better to have a crowded and useful transitory
life than a deathless one. Time, my son, I have seen the end of it.”
"I’ll remember everything,"I said.

“It is a timeless life,”he said dreamingly.“But I got lonesome for my
guitar. I’ve asked the queen, that is the mermaid, to get it back. I’m on
my way to my house now.”
“Your house is not there any more.”I said.“It disappeared years ago.”
“Did some man steal it?”he asked.

“It just rotted away with the years,” I said.“You have been gone a long
time. A war came and killed most of the young
menbbefore men before my generation. Then a plague and a famine came after, killing the rest including my own generation. What you will see here are remnants of a one vigorous race. I don’t know what will happen to us in another generation.”

“My heart beats for you,”he said sadly.“But I’ve got to go now. The
queen will be disappointed when she hears that my guitar is gone.”

“I’ve a guitar,” I said.“I want to give it to you. I want you to be
happy with the queen in that timeless place.”

“Thank you, son,”he said. “You are very understanding and kind. I’ve
sacrificed my life for this town, but that is nothing. If I didn’t go with
the queen, she would have taken many of the young men in this town.”
“But why would she do that?”I asked.
“They wouldn't understand her,”he said,
“I would have understood her,”I said.

“I’m glad we understand each other,”he said.“I might want to live on
the earth again, and you could take my place.”
I remained silent.
“They wouldn’t have understood her,”he said again.“They are too human.”

"Thank you for your sacrifice,”I said.“Please give my best regards to
the queen.”

“Now, remember that mermaid are really kind and understanding,”he said.
“They are cruel sometimes because men don’t understand them. Men of the earth

p.said:
are always thinking of happiness in terms of happiness on the earth, Mer-
maids get lonesome, too.”

body.p: “I’ll always remember,” I said.

I watched him walked walk straight into the water. And the day became sud-
denly dark and murmurous. I heard the turbulent lashing and roaring of
the water in the momentary darkness. And when the sun came out the man was
gone, forever.

And the mermaid never came out of the secret depths again. Sometimes
the townspeople could hear the faraway sound of a guitar rising from the
river when the moon was full in the summer sky.
